reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Goldman-Cecil Medicine
clinicalPearls: A rare but serious complication of warfarin, typically arising within the first few days of starting treatment
Presents with painful erythema progressing to haemorrhagic bullae and skin necrosis, favouring fatty areas such as the breasts, buttocks and thighs
It reflects a transient hypercoagulable state caused by rapid depletion of the vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulant protein C
Underlying protein C or protein S deficiency predisposes to the reaction
The risk is increased by large loading doses of warfarin without concurrent parenteral anticoagulation
Overlapping with a parenteral anticoagulant (such as heparin) when initiating warfarin reduces the risk in susceptible patients
Management includes stopping warfarin, giving vitamin K, providing alternative anticoagulation and, in protein C deficiency, protein C or fresh frozen plasma replacement
It must be distinguished from heparin-induced skin necrosis and calciphylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and of the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S. Because protein C has a short half-life, similar to that of factor VII, its anticoagulant activity falls rapidly in the first days of treatment, before the procoagulant factors with longer half-lives are fully depleted. This creates a transient net hypercoagulable state, which is exaggerated in patients with pre-existing protein C (or protein S) deficiency and by large initial doses. The resulting thrombosis of dermal and subcutaneous small vessels causes ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction and full-thickness skin necrosis in areas rich in subcutaneous fat. Concurrent parenteral anticoagulation during initiation bridges this vulnerable period.
additionalDifferentials: Heparin-induced skin necrosis and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis
Purpura fulminans from sepsis or severe protein C deficiency
Cholesterol or other embolic skin necrosis
additionalInvestigations: Protein C and protein S activity (interpreted with awareness of warfarin effect)
Platelet count and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia testing where relevant
Skin biopsy showing dermal vessel thrombosis without vasculitis
Assessment for underlying malignancy or antiphospholipid syndrome
redFlags: Extensive full-thickness necrosis requiring surgical debridement
Signs of systemic thrombosis or purpura fulminans
Necrosis over the breast, buttock or thigh appearing soon after warfarin initiation
reference.prognosis: Early recognition and treatment can limit tissue loss, but established necrosis may require debridement or reconstructive surgery and can cause significant morbidity. Prompt correction of the coagulopathy and appropriate anticoagulation improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Using large warfarin loading doses without bridging parenteral anticoagulation in at-risk patients
Interpreting protein C and S levels without accounting for the warfarin effect
Mistaking the lesions for infection and delaying anticoagulation review
Failing to provide protein C or plasma replacement in known protein C deficiency
